foundations-functions.prediction: Which fiber loses an input and which gains it if $f(0)$ changes from $0$ to $1$?
foundations-functions.objects: A function from $X=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}$ to $Y=\{0,1,2\}$; input equivalence is congruence modulo $m$.
foundations-functions.invariant: Every input has exactly one output; the nonempty fibers partition $X$.

foundations-fibers.prediction: Change $f(4)$ to $0$: predict the sizes of the fibers of $0$ and $1$.
foundations-fibers.counterexample: Assign every input output $0$; surjectivity fails but the nonempty fiber still partitions $X$.

foundations-quotient-rules.question: When does $[x]\mapsto f(x)$ survive a different representative?
foundations-quotient-rules.prediction: With $f(x)=x\bmod3$ and parity input classes, compare representatives $0$ and $2$.
foundations-quotient-rules.objects: Domain quotient $X/{\sim}$, where $\sim$ is congruence modulo $m$; the target $Y$ is not quotiented.
foundations-quotient-rules.invariant: A well-defined map must be constant on each chosen input class.
foundations-quotient-rules.debrief: A finite witness disproves the proposed rule. Absence of a witness certifies only this displayed finite domain; the lesson proves the general criterion.

mh2220-axioms.prediction: Before choosing subtraction modulo $3$, predict which axiom will fail.
mh2220-axioms.objects: Finite set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$; operation choices are modular addition, multiplication, subtraction, or unreduced addition.
mh2220-axioms.debrief: Exhaustive checks prove the axioms for the displayed finite operation. A family-wide result needs the algebraic proof in the lesson.

mh2220-inverse-order.prediction: In $C_{12}$ choose $8$: will its order be $3$, $6$ or $12$?
mh2220-inverse-order.objects: Additive $C_n$ with a chosen residue generator and its additive inverse.
mh2220-inverse-order.invariant: A word evaluates by addition modulo $n$; the first positive return is $n/\gcd(n,g)$.
mh2220-inverse-order.counterexample: Choose $4$ in $C_{12}$: a nonzero element has order $3$ and does not generate all twelve elements.

mh2220-generators.prediction: For $g=4$ in $C_{12}$ predict the reachable set; then test $r^3=e$ and $srs=r^{-1}$ in $S_3$.
mh2220-generators.objects: Additive $C_n$ with $g$ and $-g$, plus $S_3$ with $r=(123)$, $s=(12)$; products in $S_3$ apply the right factor first.
mh2220-generators.invariant: BFS records shortest words. The $S_3$ relations yield six normal forms only after a reduction argument; observed identity words alone are not a completeness proof.
mh2220-generators.counterexample: $\langle4\rangle\cup\langle6\rangle$ in $C_{12}$ omits $10$ although their join contains it; a sampled relation without normal forms does not present an arbitrary group.
mh2220-generators.debrief: The cyclic graph proves finite reachability for the selected $C_n$. The $S_3$ table checks three defining relations; a separate normal-form upper bound plus six distinct images proves that particular presentation complete.
mh2220-generators.fallback: Reachability, shortest lengths, $C_n$ subgroups, $S_3$ words, relations and normal forms are all available in labelled text and tables.

mh2220-cyclic.question: Which residues generate $C_n$?
mh2220-cyclic.prediction: Compare $4$ and $5$ in $C_{12}$: which gives all twelve points?
mh2220-cyclic.objects: Additive $C_n$ with $n\in\{6,8,12\}$, a chosen residue $g$, shortest $\pm g$ words and every divisor-order subgroup.
mh2220-cyclic.invariant: $\operatorname{ord}(g)=n/\gcd(n,g)$; one subgroup of each divisor order is listed with every element.
mh2220-cyclic.counterexample: In $C_{12}$, $\langle4\rangle\cup\langle6\rangle$ is not a subgroup, while their join is $\langle2\rangle$.
mh2220-cyclic.debrief: The finite table shows every subgroup for the selected $C_n$ and the current first-return relation. The exponent/least-positive-return proof in the lesson establishes the classification for all cyclic groups.

mh2220-cosets.objects: $S_3$ acts on three letters; permutation products apply the right factor first.
mh2220-cosets.debrief: The tiling is a complete finite example. Translation $h\mapsto ah$ proves equal coset cardinality for arbitrary groups.

mh2220-lagrange.objects: $G=S_3$ and one of four explicitly listed subgroups.
mh2220-lagrange.debrief: This partition illustrates Lagrange. It does not prove a converse; the lesson gives the $A_4$ counterexample to subgroup existence for every divisor.

mh2220-normal.prediction: For $A_3$, predict whether conjugating a $3$-cycle by a transposition fixes that element or swaps it.
mh2220-normal.objects: $S_3$, a chosen subgroup $H$ and a conjugating permutation $a$; $ab$ applies $b$ first.
mh2220-normal.invariant: Normality is equality $aHa^{-1}=H$ for every $a$, not pointwise fixation.

mh2220-quotient.prediction: Compare $H=\{e,(12)\}$ with $A_3$: predict which admits a quotient table.
mh2220-quotient.objects: Left cosets of $H\le S_3$; the product is attempted using representatives.
mh2220-quotient.invariant: A quotient table appears only for normal $H$.
mh2220-quotient.debrief: The witness rejects a nonnormal quotient. The expression $anbm=ab(b^{-1}nb)m$ explains why normality makes the general law well-defined.

mh2220-actions.objects: $S_3$ acting on letters, on itself by left multiplication, or on itself by conjugation.
mh2220-actions.invariant: The identity acts trivially and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$ for each action.

mh2220-orbit-stabilizer.objects: Left actions of $S_3$ on three letters or its six elements.
mh2220-orbit-stabilizer.counterexample: A fixed point has orbit size one and stabilizer all of $G$, even in a faithful action.
mh2220-orbit-stabilizer.debrief: The bijection $gG_x\mapsto g\cdot x$ explains the formula. The table enumerates this finite example and displays all hypotheses.

actions-faithful-transitive.prediction: For conjugation on $S_3$, predict the kernel and the orbit of identity.
actions-faithful-transitive.objects: $S_3$ acting on its elements by conjugation, or the natural and regular actions for comparison.
actions-faithful-transitive.counterexample: Conjugation on $S_3$ is faithful but not transitive.
actions-faithful-transitive.debrief: The kernel is the center for conjugation; $S_3$ has trivial center. One fixed point does not mean every group element acts trivially everywhere.

actions-stabilizer-kernel-core.objects: $S_3$ with a left action; the core is the intersection of conjugates of the selected point stabilizer.
actions-stabilizer-kernel-core.counterexample: At the identity conjugation orbit, the core is $S_3$ while the whole-action kernel is $\{e\}$.

actions-regular-conjugation.prediction: Apply $(12)$ to $e$ under regular multiplication and under conjugation.
actions-regular-conjugation.objects: $S_3$ acting on itself by $g\cdot x=gx$ or $g\cdot x=gxg^{-1}$.
actions-regular-conjugation.counterexample: Identity is a singleton conjugacy class but its regular orbit is all of $S_3$.

m3220-modules.prediction: Choose $n$, scalar $r$, a submodule generator, a vector and a learning stage. Predict the selected invariant before revealing it.
m3220-modules.objects: One left $\mathbb Z$-module $M=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ carried through action, presentation, submodule/quotient, and exactness stages.
m3220-modules.invariant: The left action is typed by $\mathbb Z\to\operatorname{End}(M)$; $\operatorname{im}(\times r)\cong M/\ker(\times r)$, while a section is needed for splitting.
m3220-modules.counterexample: $2$ is a nonunit of $\mathbb Z$ but acts invertibly on $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$; $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times6}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\to0$ is exact and nonsplit.

modules-generators.prediction: Choose $n$, scalar $r$, a submodule generator, a vector and a learning stage. Predict the selected invariant before revealing it.
modules-generators.objects: One left $\mathbb Z$-module $M=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ carried through action, presentation, submodule/quotient, and exactness stages.
modules-generators.invariant: The left action is typed by $\mathbb Z\to\operatorname{End}(M)$; $\operatorname{im}(\times r)\cong M/\ker(\times r)$, while a section is needed for splitting.
modules-generators.counterexample: $2$ is a nonunit of $\mathbb Z$ but acts invertibly on $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$; $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times6}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\to0$ is exact and nonsplit.

m3220-annihilator.prediction: Choose $n$, scalar $r$, a submodule generator, a vector and a learning stage. Predict the selected invariant before revealing it.
m3220-annihilator.objects: One left $\mathbb Z$-module $M=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ carried through action, presentation, submodule/quotient, and exactness stages.
m3220-annihilator.invariant: The left action is typed by $\mathbb Z\to\operatorname{End}(M)$; $\operatorname{im}(\times r)\cong M/\ker(\times r)$, while a section is needed for splitting.
m3220-annihilator.counterexample: $2$ is a nonunit of $\mathbb Z$ but acts invertibly on $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$; $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times6}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z\to0$ is exact and nonsplit.

orthogonal-axis-angle.prediction: For axis $(1,1,1)$, compare $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ cube preservation; then try a general nonzero axis.
orthogonal-axis-angle.objects: Any nonzero real axis vector in $\mathbb R^3$, a continuous angle from $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$, and the cube vertex set.
orthogonal-axis-angle.counterexample: $60^\circ$ about $(1,1,1)$, or $60^\circ$ about $(1,2,0)$, preserves Euclidean geometry but has no cube-group permutation or word.
orthogonal-axis-angle.debrief: The matrix and dashed axis follow the selected real vector and angle. Exact matrix matching identifies cube symmetries; the $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ ambiguity and the general proof are explained in the lesson.

representations-real-complex.name: Real and complex $C_3$ representation
representations-real-complex.prediction: Predict whether the real $120^\circ$ rotation has a real invariant line, then compare its two complex eigenlines.
representations-real-complex.objects: $C_3$ acting on a two-dimensional real space by a $120^\circ$ rotation, then its complexification on $\mathbb C^2$.
representations-real-complex.counterexample: A real irreducible plane can split into two complex one-dimensional subspaces.
representations-real-complex.debrief: $C_3$ on a two-dimensional space. Switching the scalar field preserves the group and matrix; there is no extra fixed axis. This experiment tests the displayed example; the lesson supplies the general argument.

linear-quotient.objects: A two-dimensional vector space over the selected finite field and a linear map on columns.
linear-quotient.counterexample: A noninvertible map may have several inputs with the same output, while targets outside its image have empty fibers.

mh2220-semidirect.name: $C_3\rtimes C_2$ product constructor
mh2220-semidirect.question: How can $C_3$ and $C_2$ produce either $S_3$ or $C_6$?
mh2220-semidirect.objects: Pairs in $C_3\times C_2$ with left action $\alpha:C_2\to\operatorname{Aut}(C_3)$; $b$ acts on the next rotation coordinate.
mh2220-semidirect.invariant: $\alpha(s)^2=\operatorname{id}$ and $\alpha(s)$ is invertible; the normal $C_3$ and complementary $C_2$ yield a split extension.
mh2220-semidirect.counterexample: The zero endomorphism is not an automorphism or a valid $C_2$ action; $C_4$ is a nonsplit $C_2$ extension.
mh2220-semidirect.debrief: The six-element table tests $S_3$ or $C_6$. Associativity in general uses $\alpha(hk)=\alpha(h)\alpha(k)$; internal splitting uses normality, trivial intersection and generation.

ureca-character-bound-kernel.prediction: For the $D_8$ half-turn $r^2$, predict $\chi(r^2)$, $|\chi(r^2)|$ and whether $r^2$ is in the kernel.
ureca-character-bound-kernel.objects: The faithful degree-two complexified square representation of $D_8$; $r^2$ acts as $-I_2$.
ureca-character-bound-kernel.invariant: For finite-order matrices, $|\chi(g)|\le\mathrm{degree}$; equality means scalar image, while $\chi(g)=\mathrm{degree}$ means identity image.
ureca-character-bound-kernel.counterexample: The central half-turn has $|\chi|=2$ and is not a kernel element.
ureca-character-bound-kernel.debrief: The eigenvalue argument above proves the general bound. A plotted or tabulated equality alone illustrates it; only equality of the actual trace with degree proves kernel membership.

ureca-external-tensor-products.prediction: For $\pi(a)=\omega$ on $\mathbb C$ and $\rho(r^2)=-I_2$, predict the product degree and trace at $(a,r^2)$.
ureca-external-tensor-products.objects: $C_3$-character line $V$ and $D_8$ square plane $W$ over $\mathbb C$; $(g,h)$ acts on $V\otimes W$.
ureca-external-tensor-products.counterexample: The nonidentity pair $(a,r^2)$ cancels in the $C_2\times D_8$ variant.

ureca-direct-product-irreducibles.prediction: Predict the number and degree-squared total for $C_3\times D_8$ before viewing the accounting table.
ureca-direct-product-irreducibles.objects: Irreducible complex characters of $C_3$ and $D_8$; external products form rows for $C_3\times D_8$.
ureca-direct-product-irreducibles.invariant: Inner products factor and the sum of squared product degrees is $|G||H|$.
ureca-direct-product-irreducibles.counterexample: A list of products without orthogonality cannot certify irreducibility.

ureca-product-kernel-scalar-matching.prediction: Choose $C_2$ or $C_3$ with the $D_8$ square representation. Predict whether a nonidentity product pair acts as identity.
ureca-product-kernel-scalar-matching.objects: A faithful complex character of $C_2$ or $C_3$ and the faithful degree-two $D_8$ square representation.
ureca-product-kernel-scalar-matching.invariant: A pair is in the product kernel exactly when its two operator scalars are reciprocal.
ureca-product-kernel-scalar-matching.counterexample: The pair $(a,r^2)$ lies in the $C_2\times D_8$ kernel despite both factor kernels being trivial.

ureca-faithful-direct-product.prediction: Predict the difference between $C_2\times D_8$ and $C_3\times D_8$ before checking center orders and kernel pairs.
ureca-faithful-direct-product.objects: The faithful one-dimensional $C_n$ character and faithful degree-two complex $D_8$ square representation.
ureca-faithful-direct-product.counterexample: The $C_2\times D_8$ nonidentity pair $(a,r^2)$ acts trivially, while $C_3\times D_8$ has no such pair.

mh2220-burnside.objects: A finite cyclic or dihedral group acts on labeled bead positions and hence on assignments of labeled colors.
mh2220-burnside.invariant: A coloring is fixed exactly when each permutation cycle is monochromatic; Burnside averages these counts over the whole group.
mh2220-burnside.counterexample: A nonidentity triangle rotation fixes no bead, but fixes both constant binary colorings. Naive division of $8$ by $3$ fails.
mh2220-burnside.debrief: Double-count $(g,c)$ with $g\cdot c=c$: each coloring orbit contributes $|G|$ such pairs. This proves the formula; the table checks a finite instance.

mh2220-necklaces.question: Why do six binary beads give $14$ necklaces but $13$ bracelets?
mh2220-necklaces.objects: $C_n$ acts by rotations; $D_n$ adds $n$ reflections. Colors may repeat or be unused.
mh2220-necklaces.invariant: A reflection through two opposite beads has two fixed positions and $n/2+1$ cycles; a gap-axis reflection has $n/2$ cycles.
mh2220-necklaces.counterexample: Treating all even-$n$ reflections alike gives the wrong bracelet count; dividing $2^6$ by $12$ assumes a free action.
mh2220-necklaces.debrief: Count cycles for every rotation and each reflection type, then average all $2n$ fixed-coloring counts. The table is the finite calculation.

mh2220-cycle-index.objects: The action on $n$ bead positions has cycle-index monomials $\prod_j a_j^{c_j}$. For two colors, replace $a_j$ by $x^j+y^j$.
mh2220-cycle-index.invariant: The coefficient of $x^r y^{n-r}$ after averaging counts orbits with exactly $r$ beads of the first color.
mh2220-cycle-index.counterexample: Substituting $a_j=2$ counts all binary colorings but cannot recover a prescribed inventory.
mh2220-cycle-index.debrief: Each cycle must use one color, contributing $x^j$ or $y^j$. Multiplying cycle factors and averaging is Burnside coefficient by coefficient.

mh2220-solid-colorings.objects: The $24$ orientation-preserving signed-permutation matrices act separately on cube vertices, face centers and edge midpoints.
mh2220-solid-colorings.invariant: The five proper cube rotation conjugacy classes have $1$, $6$, $3$, $8$ and $6$ elements. A class of size $m$ whose action has $c$ cycles contributes $m\cdot q^c$ fixed colorings before averaging.
mh2220-solid-colorings.counterexample: A face-axis quarter-turn fixes no vertex yet fixes $q^2$ vertex colorings. Face and vertex cycle polynomials differ.
mh2220-solid-colorings.debrief: Each matrix induces an exact permutation on the chosen feature set. The class table yields $(q^8+17q^4+6q^2)/24$ for vertices; this finite ledger illustrates Burnside.

orthogonal-metric-orientation.prediction: Predict the fixed-space dimensions of a plane reflection and $-I_3$ before comparing their matrices.
orthogonal-metric-orientation.objects: Real $\mathbb R^2$ or $\mathbb R^3$ column vectors, orthogonal matrices, coordinate-plane normals and the cube vertex set.
orthogonal-metric-orientation.invariant: $Q^TQ=I$ preserves all inner products; $\det Q$ is $\pm1$; fixed space and cube preservation are separate invariants.
orthogonal-metric-orientation.counterexample: A $37^\circ$ $z$-axis rotation preserves metric and orientation but not the cube; $-I_3$ and a plane reflection have equal determinant but different fixed spaces.
orthogonal-metric-orientation.debrief: The controls synchronize matrix, dimension, determinant, fixed space, dot-product calculation and cube verdict. The displayed examples illustrate the general identity $(Qu)\cdot(Qv)=u^TQ^TQv$, proved in the lesson.

orthogonal-plane.question: Which line does $R_\theta F$ fix, and how does $FR_\theta$ differ?
orthogonal-plane.prediction: At $\theta=0$ predict the shared fixed line, then at $\theta=90^\circ$ predict the two fixed lines of $R_\theta F$ and $FR_\theta$.
orthogonal-plane.objects: $\mathbb R^2$ column vectors, $R_\theta$ counterclockwise, and one fixed $F=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$; products apply the right factor first.
orthogonal-plane.invariant: Both products are reflections with determinant $-1$; $R_\theta F$ fixes $\theta/2$ and $FR_\theta$ fixes $-\theta/2$ modulo $180^\circ$.
orthogonal-plane.counterexample: At $\theta=90^\circ$, the two products fix $y=x$ and $y=-x$ respectively; treating the composition order as interchangeable fails.
orthogonal-plane.debrief: The graphic, selected product and exact $F$ convention agree at $\theta=0$ and throughout the slider. Matrix multiplication proves $FR_\theta F=R_{-\theta}$ and the half-angle rule; the display tests examples.
orthogonal-plane.fallback: Both matrices, selected fixed-line angle and image of $e_1$ are available as text and rendered equations.

mh2220-cayley-embedding.question: How does left multiplication turn every $S_3$ element into a distinct permutation?
mh2220-cayley-embedding.objects: $S_3$ acting on its own six elements by $\lambda_g(x)=gx$; right factor acts first in a product.
mh2220-cayley-embedding.invariant: Every $\lambda_g$ is a permutation; $\lambda_g\circ\lambda_h=\lambda_{gh}$ and $\lambda_g(e)=g$, so $\lambda$ is an injective homomorphism.
mh2220-cayley-embedding.counterexample: $S_3$ embeds into $S_6$ by its regular action but already acts faithfully on three letters; degree six is not minimal.
mh2220-cayley-embedding.fallback: Every $\lambda_g$ permutation, selected product, composition check and identity image are provided as labelled text and tables.

mh2220-sylow-existence.question: Which centralizer retains the full $p$-power in $S_3$?
mh2220-sylow-existence.prediction: Choose $p=2$ or $p=3$; predict the required Sylow subgroup order and a class whose centralizer has that $p$-part.
mh2220-sylow-existence.objects: $S_3$ conjugacy classes, centralizers and explicit Sylow subgroups.
mh2220-sylow-existence.invariant: The chosen centralizer for a class of $p$-coprime size retains the full $p$-part of $|G|$.
mh2220-sylow-existence.counterexample: A proper centralizer whose index is divisible by $p$ need not retain the full $p$-power.
mh2220-sylow-existence.debrief: The table checks one finite group. The guided proof supplies both induction branches, including a central subgroup when $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$.

mh2220-sylow-conjugacy.prediction: For $p=2$ in $S_3$, choose distinct Sylow subgroups $P$ and $Q$; predict the $P$-orbit sizes on $G/Q$ and identify a fixed coset.
mh2220-sylow-conjugacy.objects: A Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ of $S_3$ acting by left multiplication on cosets of an independently chosen Sylow subgroup $Q$.
mh2220-sylow-conjugacy.invariant: Coset count $[G:P]$ is coprime to $p$; $P$-orbit sizes are powers of $p$, so a fixed coset exists.
mh2220-sylow-conjugacy.counterexample: A set with size divisible by $p$ can consist entirely of nontrivial $p$-orbits; the fixed-point inference then fails.
mh2220-sylow-conjugacy.debrief: Fixed $gQ$ means $g^{-1}Pg\le Q$; equal Sylow orders force equality. The listed $S_3$ cosets illustrate the general proof.

mh2220-sylow-counts.question: Which Sylow counts pass arithmetic, and which occur in $S_3$?
mh2220-sylow-counts.prediction: For $p=2$ in $S_3$, list the counts satisfying $n_2\mid3$ and $n_2\equiv1\pmod2$; predict the actual count.
mh2220-sylow-counts.objects: $S_3$ Sylow subgroups, their normalizer and conjugation orbits.
mh2220-sylow-counts.counterexample: For $p=2$, $n_2=1$ passes arithmetic but $S_3$ has three distinct Sylow $2$-subgroups.

m3220-ideals.question: Which ideals survive when we quotient by $I$?
m3220-ideals.prediction: Choose an ideal of $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb F_2[X]$; predict which larger ideals correspond to ideals of the quotient.
m3220-ideals.objects: An ideal $I$ in $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb F_2[X]$, its quotient $R/I$, and every displayed ideal $J$ containing $I$.
m3220-ideals.invariant: $J\supseteq I$ corresponds to $J/I$; multiplication of classes is independent of representatives only for a two-sided ideal.
m3220-ideals.counterexample: The constants $H=\{0,1\}$ in $\mathbb F_2[X]$ are an additive subgroup, but $X\cdot1\notin H$, so multiplication of proposed classes is not well-defined.
m3220-ideals.debrief: The tables compute finite examples and their inclusion order. The general correspondence comes from ideal preimages under $R\to R/I$; two-sided absorption proves multiplication descends.

m3220-quotient-ring.prediction: Select $I$ in $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb F_2[X]$. Predict the quotient classes and whether a non-ideal additive subgroup could work.
m3220-quotient-ring.objects: Cosets of a chosen two-sided ideal, with explicit arithmetic in $\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb F_2[X]/(q)$.
m3220-quotient-ring.invariant: For $i,j\in I$, $(a+i)(b+j)-ab=aj+ib+ij\in I$; units and zero divisors are computed in the quotient.
m3220-quotient-ring.counterexample: For constants $H\subset\mathbb F_2[X]$, $X$ and $X+1$ differ by $1\in H$ but their products with $X$ differ by $X\notin H$.

m3220-polynomial-division.prediction: For $f=X^3+1$ and $g=X^2+1$ over $\mathbb Z$, predict the quotient and remainder. Then open the workbench to change either polynomial or the coefficient ring.
m3220-polynomial-division.objects: The initial dividend is $X^3+1$ and divisor is $X^2+1$ over $\mathbb Z$; after predicting, choose other coefficients or a finite coefficient ring.
m3220-polynomial-division.invariant: Each successful cancellation leaves $f=qg+r$; the remainder degree falls below the divisor degree.
m3220-polynomial-division.counterexample: Over $\mathbb Z[X]$, dividing $X$ by $2X+1$ requires the unavailable coefficient $1/2$. A field permits it, while a monic divisor works over any commutative coefficient ring.

m3220-gauss.objects: Worked polynomials in $\mathbb Q[X]$, $\mathbb R[X]$, $\mathbb C[X]$ and $\mathbb F_2[X]$, with integer content tracked before coefficient reduction.
m3220-gauss.invariant: A factorisation is valid only over its selected field; an irreducibility claim needs a degree or valid certificate under its hypotheses.
m3220-gauss.counterexample: $X^4+3X^2+2$ has no rational root but factors as $(X^2+1)(X^2+2)$; a failed Eisenstein test is inconclusive.

m3220-eisenstein.objects: Worked polynomials in $\mathbb Q[X]$, $\mathbb R[X]$, $\mathbb C[X]$ and $\mathbb F_2[X]$, with integer content tracked before coefficient reduction.
m3220-eisenstein.invariant: A factorisation is valid only over its selected field; an irreducibility claim needs a degree or valid certificate under its hypotheses.
m3220-eisenstein.counterexample: $X^4+3X^2+2$ has no rational root but factors as $(X^2+1)(X^2+2)$; a failed Eisenstein test is inconclusive.

m3220-irreducibility-tests.objects: Worked polynomials in $\mathbb Q[X]$, $\mathbb R[X]$, $\mathbb C[X]$ and $\mathbb F_2[X]$, with integer content tracked before coefficient reduction.
m3220-irreducibility-tests.invariant: A factorisation is valid only over its selected field; an irreducibility claim needs a degree or valid certificate under its hypotheses.
m3220-irreducibility-tests.counterexample: $X^4+3X^2+2$ has no rational root but factors as $(X^2+1)(X^2+2)$; a failed Eisenstein test is inconclusive.

m3220-fractions.objects: Reduced fractions in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\mathbb Z[1/3]$ and $\mathbb Q$, plus selected multiplicative subsets of $\mathbb Z$.
m3220-fractions.invariant: A reduced denominator decides membership; a map factors through $S^{-1}R$ exactly when its target makes every $s\in S$ a unit.
m3220-fractions.counterexample: In $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ with $S=\{1,2,4\}$, $1/1$ and $4/1$ become equivalent after an $S$-annihilator, although direct cross products differ.

m3220-localization.objects: Reduced fractions in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\mathbb Z[1/3]$ and $\mathbb Q$, plus selected multiplicative subsets of $\mathbb Z$.
m3220-localization.invariant: A reduced denominator decides membership; a map factors through $S^{-1}R$ exactly when its target makes every $s\in S$ a unit.
m3220-localization.counterexample: In $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ with $S=\{1,2,4\}$, $1/1$ and $4/1$ become equivalent after an $S$-annihilator, although direct cross products differ.

m3220-prime-localization.question: Which reduced fractions are absent, units or nonunits in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$?
m3220-prime-localization.objects: Reduced fractions in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\mathbb Z[1/3]$ and $\mathbb Q$, plus selected multiplicative subsets of $\mathbb Z$.
m3220-prime-localization.invariant: A reduced denominator decides membership; a map factors through $S^{-1}R$ exactly when its target makes every $s\in S$ a unit.
m3220-prime-localization.counterexample: In $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ with $S=\{1,2,4\}$, $1/1$ and $4/1$ become equivalent after an $S$-annihilator, although direct cross products differ.

m3220-noetherian.objects: Ascending, descending and prime-ideal chains in $\mathbb Z$, $F[X_1,X_2,\ldots]$, $F[X,Y]$ and $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$.
m3220-noetherian.counterexample: $\mathbb Z$ is infinite and Noetherian, while $(X_1)\subsetneq(X_1,X_2)\subsetneq\cdots$ never stabilizes in the infinite-variable ring.

m3220-submodules.prediction: For $T=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$ on $\mathbb R^2$, predict whether the $x$-axis is stable and what $T$ induces on the quotient by it. Then change the operator.
m3220-submodules.objects: The initial left $\mathbb R[t]$-module $\mathbb R^2$ has $t$ acting by $T=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$, with $W$ the $x$-axis.
m3220-submodules.invariant: $T(W)\subseteq W$ gives stability under every $p(T)$, and the quotient action remembers only the $y$-coordinate.
m3220-submodules.counterexample: The line $\mathbb R(e_1+e_2)$ is not stable under $\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$: its image $2e_1+e_2$ is not on that line. Stability under one operator does not imply stability under an unrelated operator.
m3220-submodules.debrief: The vector diagram checks one operator state. General quotient well-definedness needs submodule closure under every scalar, and $M/\ker f\cong\operatorname{im}f$ is proved in the guided lesson.
m3220-submodules.fallback: The matrix, vector image, invariant $x$-axis and induced quotient scalar are labelled in text next to the diagram.

foundations-linear-algebra.debrief: Checking a generating set proves this finite $D_8$ case. General claims require generator and field hypotheses stated in the lesson.

ureca-linear-action.question: Why do $D_8$ generator matrices give an invertible left action?
ureca-linear-action.objects: $D_8$ acts from the left on column vectors in $\mathbb F^2$ through $R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $S=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$.
ureca-linear-action.invariant: $R^4=S^2=I$ and $SRS=R^{-1}$; group inverses map to inverse matrices.
ureca-linear-action.counterexample: The $\mathbb C$ rotation eigenline fails under reflection; $I$ and a singular matrix fail the intertwiner equation.
ureca-linear-action.debrief: Checking a generating set proves this finite $D_8$ case. General claims require generator and field hypotheses stated in the lesson.

representations-characters.name: $S_3$ character construction studio
representations-characters.question: How do representation traces construct the complete $S_3$ character table?
representations-characters.objects: Complex left representations of $S_3$ on one- and two-dimensional spaces; class sizes $1,3,2$.
representations-characters.counterexample: Equal column weights give $\langle\mathrm{Std},\mathrm{Std}\rangle=5/3$ rather than one.
representations-characters.debrief: The displayed $S_3$ rows come from representations. Orthogonality for all finite groups requires its separate proof; Maschke and Schur retain their field hypotheses.

odyssey-induction.name: $S_3$ induction and reciprocity workbench
odyssey-induction.prediction: Choose an $H$-character, acting element, coset basis vector and $G$ target; predict motion, trace and both Hom dimensions.
odyssey-induction.objects: $G=S_3$, $H=\langle(12)\rangle\cong C_2$, transversal $e,r,r^2$ and one-dimensional trivial or sign $H$-character over $\mathbb C$.
odyssey-induction.invariant: $\dim\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\varphi=3$; the same $H$-correction determines generator matrices and induced trace; Frobenius reciprocity equates Hom dimensions.
odyssey-induction.counterexample: Omitting $\mathrm{sign}_H(s)=-1$ changes the $s$ trace from $-1$ to $+1$ and misidentifies $\operatorname{Ind}\mathrm{sign}_H$ as $\operatorname{Ind}\mathrm{trivial}_H$.
odyssey-induction.debrief: Coset matrices and Hom dimensions verify this $S_3$ case; the natural Hom-space isomorphism in the lesson proves Frobenius reciprocity generally.

algebra-wedderburn.prediction: Choose $M_2(F)$, $T_2(F)$ or $F[C_2]$, a coefficient field and matrix units; predict radical, quotient blocks and splitting before revealing.
algebra-wedderburn.objects: Associative finite-dimensional unital $F$-algebras $M_2(F)$, $T_2(F)$ and $F[C_2]$; natural left modules and regular modules.
algebra-wedderburn.invariant: $M_2(F)$ has one matrix block and regular multiplicity two; $T_2(F)$ has radical $FE_{12}$ and a nonsplit natural module; $F[C_2]$ changes in characteristic two.
algebra-wedderburn.counterexample: Simple successive layers of the natural $T_2(F)$-module do not split: $E_{12}$ sends $e_2$ to $e_1$.

tensor-products.prediction: Choose cyclic right/left $\mathbb Z$-modules, scalar and vectors; predict gcd generator order and both balanced expressions.
tensor-products.objects: $U=\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$ as a right $\mathbb Z$-module and $V=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ as a left $\mathbb Z$-module with $t=[1]\otimes[1]$.
tensor-products.counterexample: $(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z)=0$ despite two nonzero factors; a rank-two tensor sum is not pure.
tensor-products.debrief: The cyclic calculation illustrates the universal property. Arbitrary-ring existence follows from the quotient construction in the lesson; external $\boxtimes$ also carries a product-group action.

mh2220-direct-product.objects: Pairs in $C_3\times C_2$ with left action $\alpha:C_2\to\operatorname{Aut}(C_3)$; $b$ acts on the next rotation coordinate.
mh2220-direct-product.invariant: $\alpha(s)^2=\operatorname{id}$ and $\alpha(s)$ is invertible; the normal $C_3$ and complementary $C_2$ yield a split extension.
mh2220-direct-product.counterexample: The zero endomorphism is not an automorphism or a valid $C_2$ action; $C_4$ is a nonsplit $C_2$ extension.
mh2220-direct-product.debrief: The six-element table tests $S_3$ or $C_6$. Associativity in general uses $\alpha(hk)=\alpha(h)\alpha(k)$; internal splitting uses normality, trivial intersection and generation.

characters-burnside.objects: A finite group $G$ of order $p^a q^b$; the $S_3$ conjugacy classes are a concrete index example.
characters-burnside.invariant: For $z$ in the center of a Sylow $q$-subgroup, $q^b\mid |C_G(z)|$, so $|z^G|$ is a $p$-power.
characters-burnside.debrief: The displayed chain proves the reduction to the imported character-theoretic class-size lemma and then induction; the $S_3$ table is an illustration, not a proof of that lemma.

m3220-nilradical.prediction: Predict the powers of $2$ in $\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z$ and whether the same radical claim holds for $M_2(\mathbb F_2)$.
m3220-nilradical.objects: Commutative unital finite rings $\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$; noncommutative $M_2(\mathbb F_2)$ as a failure state.
m3220-nilradical.invariant: In commutative unital rings $\operatorname{Nil}(R)$ is the prime-ideal intersection; in the Artinian cases $J=\operatorname{Nil}$ and a uniform power of $J$ vanishes.
m3220-nilradical.counterexample: $E_{12}$ is nilpotent in $M_2(\mathbb F_2)$ but $J(M_2(\mathbb F_2))=0$.
